mcq.stem: Sylvie wants to see how loudly she can play her music without her parents hearing it. Sylvie’s goal is most closely related to which of the following terms?
mcq.answer_text: Absolute threshold is the ability to detect a stimulus half the time and is defined as the lowest level of stimulation a person can sense. In a sense, the absolute threshold is also an example of a just-noticeable difference, also called the difference threshold, but absolute threshold is a more specific and therefore better answer to this question.

mcq.stem: Lately, Petunia has been experiencing some visual hallucinations. Which part of her cerebral cortex is most likely to be involved?
mcq.context: Petunia is a professional boxer who has endured some hard hits to her head.
mcq.answer_text: The primary visual cortex is located in the occipital lobe of the brain; therefore, that is the part of the cortex most likely to be involved in visual hallucinations.

mcq.stem: Petunia’s doctor sends her for some tests including one in which electric sensors are put all over her head to detect a series of waves. What type of test does this describe?
mcq.context: Petunia is a professional boxer who has endured some hard hits to her head.
mcq.answer_text: EEG stands for electroencephalogram, and this method uses sensors to detect electrical signals in the brain and convert them into waves.

mcq.stem: Petunia sees a neurologist who specializes in sports-related head trauma. Dr. Lazarus invites her to be in a small study he is running on four other athletes. Petunia agrees. She fills out a large battery of surveys and then signs up for several in-depth interviews as well as a full battery of tests. How would you describe Dr. Lazarus’s study?
mcq.context: Petunia is a professional boxer who has endured some hard hits to her head.
mcq.answer_text: Case studies focus on one person or on a small group of people with the goal of obtaining a rich and deep understanding of a few cases rather than a more general understanding of a larger sample.

mcq.stem: Jodi has been swimming competitively for four years. She gets up at 5 a.m. every day to swim two hours before school. On weekends, she swims at least five hours a day. According to the Big Five model of personality, Jodi has high
mcq.answer_text: All the listed terms are traits associated with the Big Five. Jodi appears to be quite conscientious—or hardworking—given her commitment to such a demanding practice schedule.

mcq.stem: Penny sends Leonard to the grocery store to pick up a few things. Assuming he doesn’t write down a list of what she wants or engage in some elaborative rehearsal, approximately how many items will he remember to buy?
mcq.answer_text: Seven is the average number of items people are able to keep in their short-term memories, so it is likely Leonard will be able to recall that number of items.

mcq.stem: Dr. Krebs studies the relationships between pets and their human companions. She wants to know if children raised in families with pets grow up to be more empathetic and compassionate. The graph below shows the data she collected in a recent study of nearly 100 people who grew up with pets. From the data, Dr. Krebs concludes that living with cats leads people to be more compassionate. Which of the following statements provides the most valid criticism of this conclusion?

options.A: It would take a much larger sample to demonstrate this.
options.B: It’s not possible to measure a trait like compassion accurately.
options.C: The participants weren’t randomly assigned to conditions.
options.D: The description does not say if the difference between groups was significant.

mcq.answer_text: Since Dr. Krebs compared people who grew up with cats to people who did not, she was unable to randomly assign them to conditions. Therefore, there may be other differences between these groups of people that prevent her from being able to conclude that growing up with cats affects people in any particular way. Dr. Krebs’s study is an example of an ex post facto design. So she can conclude that there is a difference between these groups but not definitively conclude that growing up with cats caused this difference.

mcq.stem: The interviews are more likely than the surveys to yield
mcq.context: Paola has been studying a group of approximately 100 women for the past 30 years to see how their ideas about gender discrimination have changed. Every five years, she sends them a survey made up of Likert-type items, and she interviews a small subset of the women and records their responses to open-ended questions.
mcq.answer_text: Qualitative data can be words, sentences, or paragraphs that result from interviews or focus groups. In contrast, quantitative data are numerical.

mcq.stem: Paola’s research design is best classified as
mcq.context: Paola has been studying a group of approximately 100 women for the past 30 years to see how their ideas about gender discrimination have changed. Every five years, she sends them a survey made up of Likert-type items, and she interviews a small subset of the women and records their responses to open-ended questions.
mcq.answer_text: Since the research has extended over such a long period of time (30 years), it would be classified as longitudinal.

mcq.stem: One of the greatest challenges in this type of research is that

options.A: people’s opinions are likely to change over the course of 30 years.
options.B: as time passes, some participants are likely to drop out of the study.
options.D: the passage of time creates a confounding variable.

mcq.context: Paola has been studying a group of approximately 100 women for the past 30 years to see how their ideas about gender discrimination have changed. Every five years, she sends them a survey made up of Likert-type items, and she interviews a small subset of the women and records their responses to open-ended questions.
mcq.answer_text: An issue in longitudinal studies is that the sample with which the researcher begins is highly unlikely to be the same as the sample when the data collection ends. Participants may pass away, move, or simply stop responding. People’s opinions are likely to change over time—and that’s the goal of studying something over a long period of time. If the expressed opinions change because the composition of the sample changes, that is a problem.

mcq.stem: Winston has sought help for feelings of anxiety from a counseling psychologist. This psychologist, Dr. Sunu, suggests that Winston’s anxiety is likely linked to a genetic predisposition. Based on this view, Dr. Sunu would best be classified as a(n)
mcq.answer_text: Evolutionary psychologists attribute much of human experience to genetic influences.

mcq.stem: Luis was in a terrible car accident, and his doctors think that he hit his head on the window during the crash. Even months after the accident, Luis continues to have difficulty speaking. Which part of his brain was most likely damaged in the accident?
mcq.answer_text: The cerebral cortex is the part of the brain that controls complex thought and behavior, including language.

mcq.stem: Four-year-old Petra and her family have several indoor-outdoor house cats. On a recent trip to Costa Rica on a jungle tour, they saw an oncilla, the smallest wild cat that lives in that country. Delighted, Petra asked, “Whose kitty is that?” Petra’s belief that the oncilla was a domestic cat is an example of
mcq.answer_text: Petra used her existing schema of a cat (kitty) to try to figure out what the oncilla was. If she is corrected and told about what an oncilla actually is, she will likely accommodate her schema to exclude any small cats found in the Costa Rican jungle.

mcq.stem: Which of the following are the main ethical concerns an IRB would want Giovanni to address?

options.A: Protecting participants from psychological and physical harm
options.B: Protecting confidentiality and protecting participants from psychological harm
options.C: Protecting participants from physical harm and obtaining informed consent
options.D: Protecting confidentiality and obtaining informed consent

mcq.context: For his college Introduction to Psychology class, Giovanni wants to look at whether expressions of gratitude predict subjective well- being. For two weeks when in his classes, he pays close attention to comments related to gratitude and records them and who said them in a lab notebook; he doesn’t tell people he’s doing this because he wants them to act naturally. At the end of the two weeks, Giovanni surveys his peers and records their names so that he will be able to link the data from the two parts of his study.
mcq.answer_text: Confidentiality is an important issue since Giovanni knows the participants and collects their names in order to link the two datasets. While it would be fairly easy to obtain consent for the survey part of the study, naturalistic observational studies pose issues. First, it is impossible to get people to consent to a study they don’t know about. Second, the idea that participants do not know they are being observed is central to the idea of naturalistic observation.

mcq.stem: How would you describe the research design Giovanni uses in the first phase of his study?
mcq.context: For his college Introduction to Psychology class, Giovanni wants to look at whether expressions of gratitude predict subjective well- being. For two weeks when in his classes, he pays close attention to comments related to gratitude and records them and who said them in a lab notebook; he doesn’t tell people he’s doing this because he wants them to act naturally. At the end of the two weeks, Giovanni surveys his peers and records their names so that he will be able to link the data from the two parts of his study.
mcq.answer_text: The goal of naturalistic observation is to obtain an accurate sense of how participants act by observing them unobtrusively.

mcq.stem: When the study is over, Giovanni finds no relationship between his peers’ expressions of gratitude and their subjective well- being. He tells his teacher that he knew the idea that expressions of gratitude would not be related to subjective well- being. With this statement, Giovanni is demonstrating
mcq.context: For his college Introduction to Psychology class, Giovanni wants to look at whether expressions of gratitude predict subjective well- being. For two weeks when in his classes, he pays close attention to comments related to gratitude and records them and who said them in a lab notebook; he doesn’t tell people he’s doing this because he wants them to act naturally. At the end of the two weeks, Giovanni surveys his peers and records their names so that he will be able to link the data from the two parts of his study.
mcq.answer_text: Hindsight bias is the tendency to view the outcome of something as obvious when looking back on it.

mcq.stem: Dr. Chou, a personality psychologist, is running a study to look at the factors linked to happiness. The data below depict the relationships between a number of personality characteristics and happiness. Correlation Coefficient (r- Characteristic value) Wisdom 0.6 Courage 0.4 Intelligence 0.1 Extraversion –0.2 Narcissism –0.8 Justice 0.4 Based on the values presented in the table, knowledge of which trait will best enable the prediction of someone’s happiness level?
mcq.answer_text: Correlations range from 0 (no correlation) to 1 or –1, which are equally strong correlations that denote direct and inverse relationships, respectively. Since –0.8 is the furthest number from 0, the correlation between happiness and narcissism is the strongest correlation of the ones presented—it just happens to show an inverse relationship where greater happiness is associated with lower levels of narcissism.

mcq.stem: Simi is an elementary school student. He has just mastered the multiplication tables and is in the process of trying out for a travel soccer team. According to the psychosocial theory of development, Simi is most likely in which stage?
mcq.answer_text: Between ages 6 and 12, the psychosocial theory of development suggests that people grapple with a fundamental task of establishing a sense of industry (the ability to accomplish things) and that failure to do so can result in a sense of inferiority.

mcq.stem: In this scenario, the original toy car is a(n)
mcq.context: After getting into a toy car, Kate was stung 12 times by bees that had made a nest in the car. Kate cries every time she sees the car or any other toy car.
mcq.answer_text: In this question about classical conditioning, the car is clearly a stimulus as opposed to a response. Since the car would have started out as a neutral stimulus and Kate learned to fear it when it was paired with the unconditioned stimulus of being stung, the car is an example of a conditioned stimulus.

mcq.stem: Kate’s parents want her to get over her fear of the car, so they offer her a cookie every time she touches the car. Her parents’ approach is based on which type of learning?
mcq.context: After getting into a toy car, Kate was stung 12 times by bees that had made a nest in the car. Kate cries every time she sees the car or any other toy car.
mcq.answer_text: In operant conditioning, people or animals learn from the consequences of their actions. Giving Kate a cookie every time she touches the car would be an example of positive reinforcement, which should make it more likely that she touches the car again.

mcq.stem: When the offer of the cookie doesn’t work, Kate’s parents put Kate’s little brother Eli into the car to show how much fun it is. Unfortunately, as soon as he’s put into the car, Eli bursts into tears. How did Eli learn to fear the car?
mcq.context: After getting into a toy car, Kate was stung 12 times by bees that had made a nest in the car. Kate cries every time she sees the car or any other toy car.
mcq.answer_text: Modeling, or observational learning, takes place when one person or animal watches another of the same species engage in a behavior and then mimics that behavior. Eli has watched Kate react to the car and has learned to fear it.

mcq.stem: For three months, Kiki has to wear a patch over one eye to strengthen the muscles in his other eye. During that time, which of the following depth cues will he be unable to use?
mcq.answer_text: Convergence is a bipolar depth cue, which means that it requires the use of two eyes; the other three choices are all monocular depth cues that Kiki should be able to use despite the eye patch.

mcq.stem: “Read pages 224 to pages 228 for homework,” says Mr. Gupta. Elise repeats “224 to 228” in her mind until she can write it down. The part of memory most closely associated with this scenario is
mcq.answer_text: The repetition of the sound of some information keeps it in the phonological loop, a part of working memory.

mcq.stem: Simone finds herself frequently panicked when surprising things happen. What part of the peripheral nervous system likely accounts for Simone’s reactions?
mcq.answer_text: The sympathetic nervous system, which is part of the autonomic nervous system, plays an important role in arousing the body in response to potential threats.

mcq.stem: At a party, Sonya takes a drug that mimics the effect of dopamine on the brain. This drug can best be classified as a(n)
mcq.answer_text: Agonists are chemicals that are similar enough in structure to something that occurs naturally in the body that they can bind to the same receptors and cause similar effects as the naturally occurring agent. Agonists can be hormones or neurotransmitters, and a compound can be an endorphin agonist. However, agonists are not endorphins—the body’s natural painkillers.

mcq.stem: Which of the following situations best illustrates the sunk-cost fallacy?

options.A: Karen continues to pay for Netflix even though she can’t really afford it.
options.B: Adrian finds she dislikes dental school but continues with it because she’s already completed her first year.
options.C: Tiara sells her stock in a large corporation because its value is decreasing and she wants to invest in something else.
options.D: Kiko decides she would rather go out to dinner with a group of friends rather than attend her niece’s basketball game.

mcq.answer_text: Once people put a lot of time or effort into doing something, they are unlikely to give it up even if doing so would likely make them happier; this is called the sunk-cost fallacy. A very basic example involves waiting on a line. Even if it becomes clear that the line is impossibly long and someone would pretty much rather do anything else than wait on it, people tend to remain on the line rather than lose the time they have already invested waiting on the line even though this course of action means more time lost overall.

mcq.stem: When asked to draw a scientist, most elementary school children draw a white man in a white lab coat. This depiction is most closely related to which of the following concepts?
mcq.answer_text: A prototype is the most typical example of a category. Everyone’s prototype is probably slightly different, but they all function the same way; the prototype springs to mind when one thinks of the category. Even if we know that many different types of people of all ages, genders, races, and preferred clothing styles can be scientists, most of us have probably created a prototype based on what we have most often been exposed to, which is likely a not especially dapper, white man in a white lab coat.

mcq.stem: Implicit memory plays a large role in which of the following behaviors?

options.A: Recalling the names of the 50 U.S. states
options.C: Thinking about the last time you went to a birthday party
options.D: Working out a new, challenging algebra problem

mcq.answer_text: Implicit memories, as opposed to explicit memories, do not need to be consciously recalled. Remembering the names of the 50 states that make up the United States and thinking back on a birthday party both involve bringing information into your consciousness. Tying your shoes, on the other hand, is something we can do without conscious thought (provided that we’ve previously learned this skill). Working out a new type of problem involves problem-solving skills as well as memory.

mcq.stem: The table below provides information on five immigrants to the United States who spoke no English when they arrived. The table includes their age when they arrived in the country, how long they have been here, and a fluency score that assesses their English skills from 1 (weakest) to 9 (strongest). Age at Length of Time in Immigration U.S. Fluency Score Monique 16 14 7 Alberto 10 8 9 Lupe 4 10 9 Franz 46 12 8 Lars 24 15 6 Which statement is best supported by the data?

options.A: Age at arrival time is inversely related to fluency.
options.B: The longer someone spends in the country, the greater his or her fluency.
options.C: People who arrive before puberty tend to be more fluent.
options.D: Young adults are best at achieving fluency.

mcq.answer_text: Research shows there is a critical period for learning languages, and the data in the table support that statement. Alberto and Lupe, who immigrated at the ages of 10 and 4, respectively, are the most fluent despite having spent the least amount of time in the country.

mcq.stem: Dr. Craig studies the relationship between exposure to electronic devices and weight during childhood. In one study, he compares the findings of many studies over the last 50 years to try to draw a general, overarching conclusion. What type of study is this?
mcq.answer_text: A meta-analysis seeks to combine results across a number of similar studies.

mcq.stem: Seymour slams the door on Spike, and Spike thinks, “This guy’s a jerk!” without considering that something might have just upset Seymour, causing him to act in an uncharacteristically obnoxious manner. Spike’s thought process is an example of
mcq.answer_text: The fundamental attribution error explains that people tend to overestimate the role of someone’s personality in shaping their behavior and tend to underestimate the role of the situation. This concept is related to the actor-observer effect, which explains that we not only overestimate the role of personality when thinking about other people (when we are an observer) but that we also underestimate it when thinking of ourselves (when we are the actor).

mcq.stem: Psychodynamic theory proposes that a part of the mind known as the ego tries to protect our conscious minds from threatening thoughts using defense mechanisms. Which of the following scenarios illustrates the defense mechanism of reaction formation?

options.A: Lola loathes her sister Audrey but tells everyone she knows how much she adores Audrey.
options.B: Simeon is terrified of his grandfather but tries to emulate him.
options.C: When Evan gets angry at his parents, he breaks things in his room.
options.D: When she was six, Bella’s parents went through an ugly divorce, but Bella doesn’t remember it.

mcq.answer_text: Reaction formation is when one has an unacceptable feeling and therefore expresses its opposite.

mcq.stem: Diana has sought help from a psychologist for her feelings of anger. This psychologist, Dr. Partin, suggests that Diana’s anger is likely due to her unrealistic expectations of the world. Based on this view, Dr. Partin would best be classified as a
mcq.answer_text: Cognitive psychologists are most interested in how people think. Unrealistic expectations of how life should be could, from a cognitive perspective, result in anger.

mcq.stem: What is likely to happen when she is allowed to sleep without interruption?

options.A: She will spend all her time in REM.
options.B: She will spend more time than usual in REM.
options.C: She will spend less time than usual in REM.
options.D: She will spend nearly no time in REM.

mcq.context: Farnaz volunteers for a sleep study where she is awoken every time she appears to be starting REM sleep.
mcq.answer_text: While research suggests that we can’t make up for lost sleep (sleep debt), it has supported a phenomenon called “REM rebound” in which people deprived specifically of REM sleep tend to spend a larger portion of their time asleep in REM in subsequent nights.

mcq.stem: What method would the researchers most likely use to tell when Farnaz was entering REM?

options.A: By monitoring her level of glucose consumption

mcq.context: Farnaz volunteers for a sleep study where she is awoken every time she appears to be starting REM sleep.
mcq.answer_text: Sleep researchers rely heavily on the brain waves produced by an EEG in determining when people move through different sleep stages.

mcq.stem: Psychologists have been trying to help people who suffer from psychological disorders for many decades. The development of more kinds of and more effective medications during the last 50 years has facilitated which of the following changes in how we care for the mentally ill?

options.B: Increasing rates of people admitted as long-term patients in hospitals
options.C: Decreasing numbers of people kept in psychiatric institutions
options.D: Decreasing numbers of people becoming psychotherapists

mcq.answer_text: The increased efficacy of medications has enabled more people with severe psychiatric issues to live outside of institutions. Lobotomies are no longer performed, although other types of psychosurgery have been developed. Additionally, many people continue to seek the help of psychotherapists for a wide range of issues.

mcq.stem: Which answer reflects the humanistic perspective?
mcq.context: Lorenzo is doing a project on hard work and procrastination in teens. He interviews top students at LaForge High School and asks them to describe why they study. He then codes their responses into one of four groups as shown below. Group A B C D Theme To achieve my To get into a Family I don’t study potential good college pressure Percent of 6% 72% 14% 8% Responses
mcq.answer_text: Humanistic psychologists believe that people are driven to be the best they can. This view represents intrinsic motivation. Choices B and C, on the other hand, represent more of a behaviorist view of motivation—people do things for rewards or to avoid punishments.

mcq.stem: How would you describe the type of data collected in this study?
mcq.context: Lorenzo is doing a project on hard work and procrastination in teens. He interviews top students at LaForge High School and asks them to describe why they study. He then codes their responses into one of four groups as shown below. Group A B C D Theme To achieve my To get into a Family I don’t study potential good college pressure Percent of 6% 72% 14% 8% Responses
mcq.answer_text: The data type is clearly not numeric, so this type of data is qualitative. Qualitative data is typically thought to be less objective than quantitative data, and qualitative data cannot be standardized. The strengths of qualitative data lie in its ability to capture a deeper and richer understanding of the human experience.

mcq.stem: Hyun is a high school student. He wants to join the district-level orchestra because it will look good on his college application, but he doesn’t want to commit to the three-hour weekly practices. How would you describe Hyun’s dilemma?
mcq.answer_text: Hyun is attracted to the prestige of being in the orchestra (that’s the approach part) but is repelled by the three-hour weekly time commitment (that’s the avoidance part).

mcq.stem: Professor Jenkins researches the relationship between adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and subjective well-being in adulthood. The data from her latest study are graphed below. How would you describe the relationship graphed above?
mcq.answer_text: Because the points on the scatterplot slope from the upper left to the lower right, the relationship is negative (also known as indirect).

mcq.stem: Adam’s great-grandfather was born in the early 20th century. While listening to his great-grandfather, Adam is always amazed at how different his life would have been if he grew up when his great-grandfather did. This difference is represented by the
mcq.answer_text: The ecological system theory outlines the way various factors can affect people’s development. The one referenced in the question is the time period during which one grows up, which is the chronosystem.

mcq.stem: Feeling happy and upbeat as she started college, Lila joined new organizations and made new, close friends. These actions led her to feel fulfilled and reinforced her sense of well-being. This pattern is best explained by the
mcq.answer_text: According to the broaden-and-build theory, when you expand your skills and social networks (broaden), it aids in your overall sense of well-being.

mcq.stem: Wyatt is on medication to help control the hallucinations he’s been experiencing. One unfortunate side effect of the medication has been tardive dyskinesia. Which of the following issues is Wyatt most likely to be experiencing due to the tardive dyskinesia?

options.C: Symptoms of anxiety like a racing heart

mcq.answer_text: Tardive dyskinesia is a motor problem that is associated with tremors of the hands and other body parts as well as facial muscle contractions that may present as grimaces.

mcq.stem: Dr. Ambrose is a clinical psychologist who combines a number of techniques in her practice. These include modeling, cognitive restructuring, and reinforcement. Which of the following types of therapy is Dr. Ambrose most likely to practice?
mcq.answer_text: Dr. Ambrose is using a combination of behavioral and cognitive techniques. Dialectical-behavior therapy is an example of cognitive-behavioral therapy.

mcq.stem: After staring for a full minute at a picture of a red parrot, Stanley looks away and sees the image of a green parrot. This image will be the brightest and clearest if Stanley glances away and looks at a ___________ wall.
mcq.answer_text: The negative afterimage described occurs because some of the cells that sense color are arranged in pairs, including pairs of red and green. The original parrot appears red because it reflects mainly red wavelengths of light. By staring at something red for a full minute, the red receptors get fatigued. Objects that appear white reflect all wavelengths of light. Because the red receptors are fatigued, however, there is a brief period of time during which the green receptors respond more strongly than the red receptors, creating a brief afterimage of a green parrot.

mcq.stem: Which statement is best supported by the graph?

options.A: Older people reported more pain than younger people.
options.B: Older people are more suggestible than younger people.
options.C: Older people were less helped by hypnosis than younger people.
options.D: Older people were more fearful of hypnosis than younger people.

mcq.context: Dr. Jimenez is studying the effects of hypnosis on reported chronic pain in people in their 40s and 70s. His results are graphed below.
mcq.answer_text: Comparing the pair of bars on the left with the pair on the right shows that the participants in their 40s seemed to benefit more from the hypnosis than those in their 70s.

mcq.stem: Which theory is most relevant to Dr. Jimenez’s study?
mcq.context: Dr. Jimenez is studying the effects of hypnosis on reported chronic pain in people in their 40s and 70s. His results are graphed below.
mcq.answer_text: Gate control theory proposes an explanation for how pain signals get to the brain. Both place and frequency theories have to do with hearing. Although a number of theories deal with perception, there is not one specific perception theory in the AP Psychology curriculum.

mcq.stem: Ms. Morin teaches her students to think about how to maximize their test-taking performance by thinking about their relative strengths and weaknesses in the unit and asking themselves questions. Ms. Morin is encouraging her students to develop their
mcq.answer_text: Metacognition is defined as thinking about thinking—in other words, reflecting on how you learn and how you can maximize your learning.

mcq.stem: Riley studies for her physics test and then goes to sleep. The next morning, she takes the test during sixth period. If things she learns during the first five periods of school obscure her memory of what she studied, her performance may be hampered by
mcq.answer_text: Riley is likely to learn other things during the first five periods of the day. If that new material makes it more difficult for her to remember things she has already learned, she is experiencing retroactive interference. An example of proactive interference would be if she had difficulty learning some of the physics information because of something she already knew.

mcq.stem: Jamal’s older sister gives him five pieces of candy in a little pile, but Jamal screams that he wants more. His sister then spreads out that candy and tells him that he now has more. What is the oldest age Jamal is likely to be if he is happy with this new offer?
mcq.answer_text: According to Piaget’s cognitive theory of development, until children enter the concrete operational stage around age seven, they lack an ability known as conservation. Conservation applies not just to understanding that the number of items does not change depending on how they are arranged but also to other factors such as area and volume.

mcq.stem: During the summer of 1977, New York City experienced a massive blackout. During the blackout, especially at night, looting and other criminal acts were widespread. Which phenomenon helps explain why blackouts might result in such chaos?
mcq.answer_text: Deindividuation is a loss of self-restraint that typically occurs under conditions of anonymity and arousal. With the electricity out, people had a sense of anonymity at night that led them to act in ways they might not have under typical circumstances. Additionally, the blackout led to a sense of excitement or arousal with people pouring into the streets that may also have contributed to these antisocial behaviors.

mcq.stem: In his early 20s, Ernie is diagnosed with schizophrenia based primarily on his increasingly catatonic behavior. Ernie is most likely to

options.A: appear emotionless even in situations that would make most people very emotional.
options.B: talk a mile a minute without pausing between words and topics.
options.C: remain in a single position for long periods of time without moving.
options.D: report that he is being watched or followed.

mcq.answer_text: Catatonia is one of the symptoms of schizophrenia and affects movement. When catatonic, people with schizophrenia may remain immobile in a particular position for long periods of time. The other choices are symptoms of schizophrenia but do not represent catatonia.

mcq.stem: When Linus tells Sally that he never went anywhere without his blanket until he was a teenager, Sally shares that she never really liked her older brother. This is an example of
mcq.answer_text: Self-disclosure is a way people become emotionally closer by sharing intimate details about their lives.

mcq.stem: One day, Guy finds that an animal shelter has sent him free return address labels. Guy has never visited, donated to, or even heard of the shelter. Which of the following helps explain the shelter’s gift to Guy?
mcq.answer_text: Norms are our sense of how most people should behave, and the norms of reciprocity hold that we should reciprocate when someone does something nice for us. Charities often send or give potential donors gifts in the hope of triggering this norm and receiving a donation in return.

mcq.stem: The Kims don’t want to give their 10-year-old son a phone. However, he tells them all his friends are getting phones when they move on to middle school and that he will be a social outcast if he doesn’t have one. In fact, many people in the Kims’ community share their opposition to giving their children phones so young, but most relent in the face of their children’s insistence that they will be left out if they don’t have phones. What psychological phenomenon is best illustrated by this situation?
mcq.answer_text: A social trap results from many people taking a small action that has a tiny negative effect on the larger community but for which the collective impact is large. The more families that get their children phones early on, the more pressure and social need there is for everyone to get phones for their children.

mcq.stem: What is the range of foul shots made during games?
mcq.context: Mahin is the manager of his school’s girls’ basketball team. He collects data on foul shooting percentages for the starting five players during practices and during games. Percent of Foul Shots Made Percent of Foul Shots Made (Practices) (Games) Taylor 78% 82% Jess 64% 74% Percent of Foul Shots Made Percent of Foul Shots Made (Practices) (Games) Mya 70% 70% Olivia 57% 72% Marli 64% 70%
mcq.answer_text: The range is the difference between the highest and lowest percentages. For foul shots during a game, these percentages are 82% and 70%, making the range 82% – 70% = 12%.

mcq.stem: Which of the following statistics is larger in the dataset from practices than it is in the dataset from games?
mcq.context: Mahin is the manager of his school’s girls’ basketball team. He collects data on foul shooting percentages for the starting five players during practices and during games. Percent of Foul Shots Made Percent of Foul Shots Made (Practices) (Games) Taylor 78% 82% Jess 64% 74% Percent of Foul Shots Made Percent of Foul Shots Made (Practices) (Games) Mya 70% 70% Olivia 57% 72% Marli 64% 70%
mcq.answer_text: The standard deviation is a measure of variability, while the other three terms are measures of central tendency. Measures of variability indicate how spread out the scores in a distribution are, while measures of central tendency summarize where most of the data are as represented by a single value. You do not need to do any calculations to answer this question. The mean, median, and mode for foul shots made during games are clearly higher as four of the five players make a higher percentage of their foul shots during games as opposed to during practices; Mya performs equally across the two situations. On the other hand, the percentage of foul shots made during practices varies much more than the percentage of foul shots made during games.

mcq.stem: The difference in performance between games and practices illustrates which of the following psychological principles?
mcq.context: Mahin is the manager of his school’s girls’ basketball team. He collects data on foul shooting percentages for the starting five players during practices and during games. Percent of Foul Shots Made Percent of Foul Shots Made (Practices) (Games) Taylor 78% 82% Jess 64% 74% Percent of Foul Shots Made Percent of Foul Shots Made (Practices) (Games) Mya 70% 70% Olivia 57% 72% Marli 64% 70%
mcq.answer_text: More people typically watch games than watch practices. Social facilitation is the idea that the presence of other people improves the performance of a well-learned skill.

mcq.stem: Which statement is best supported by the data?

options.A: Many more boys are diagnosed with ADHD than girls.
options.B: Boys tend to be diagnosed earlier than girls.
options.C: Boys tend to manifest more severe symptoms than girls.
options.D: Boys are unable to hide their symptoms as well as girls.

mcq.context: Ephraim just concluded a study on people diagnosed with ADHD, and his data appear in the table below. He recruited participants from a variety of mental health organizations and support groups around his city. Average Age at Diagnosis Percent Medicated Girls 14 52% Boys 8 48%
mcq.answer_text: The table shows that boys in this study were diagnosed around age 8 while girls weren’t diagnosed until around age 14; none of the other statements are supported by the data displayed.

mcq.stem: If Ephraim finds that the difference between the percentage of boys and girls who are being medicated for ADHD is not statistically significant, it means that

options.A: the operational definitions he used were not valid.
options.B: the operational definitions he used were not reliable.
options.C: the difference between the groups is likely to be due to chance.
options.D: the difference between the groups is unlikely to be due to chance.

mcq.context: Ephraim just concluded a study on people diagnosed with ADHD, and his data appear in the table below. He recruited participants from a variety of mental health organizations and support groups around his city. Average Age at Diagnosis Percent Medicated Girls 14 52% Boys 8 48%
mcq.answer_text: If a finding is statistically significant, it means the difference is unlikely to have occurred by chance. In this case, if the difference between groups is not statistically significant, researchers conclude that the difference was likely caused by chance.

mcq.stem: Which of the following statements is supported by the data?

options.A: Some cultures are better at recognizing expressions than others.
options.B: Positive emotions are recognized better than negative emotions.
options.C: All participants were able to identify more than half of the emotions shown.
options.D: Of the emotions shown, people struggled most to identify disgust.

mcq.context: A number of researchers have proposed that some emotions are universal. Data were gathered from a cross-cultural study of over 1,200 people in 10 nations, and the percentage of people who could identify each emotion is graphed below.
mcq.answer_text: The graph shows that the percentage of people who were able to recognize disgust was smaller than the percentage who could recognize the other emotions. The data do not provide information that relates to choice (A). Choice (B) is false since more people could identify anger than any of the other emotions. The graph depicts average performance rather than the performance of individuals, so it does not provide support for choice (C).

mcq.stem: While the data suggest that people across countries and cultures may be able to recognize many of the same emotions, other research shows that they may express emotions differently. These differences are thought be caused by
mcq.context: A number of researchers have proposed that some emotions are universal. Data were gathered from a cross-cultural study of over 1,200 people in 10 nations, and the percentage of people who could identify each emotion is graphed below.
mcq.answer_text: Display rules are culture specific and relate to the conditions under which it is appropriate to express certain emotions.

mcq.stem: The doctor first has Gwen look through a number of different lenses to see if they sharpen her vision. This process would most likely help fix difficulties Gwen might be having with
mcq.context: Eight-year-old Gwen is beginning to complain of vision problems, so her parents take her to see an eye doctor. Gwen tells the doctor that everything is starting to look “fuzzy. ”
mcq.answer_text: Accommodation is the process by which the lens in the eye changes shape to focus an image on the retina. Glasses or contact lenses are used to correct vision when someone is having difficulty focusing.

mcq.stem: The doctor also dilates Gwen’s eyes to look at the back of the eye. Which type of retinal cells is the doctor most likely to be interested in?
mcq.context: Eight-year-old Gwen is beginning to complain of vision problems, so her parents take her to see an eye doctor. Gwen tells the doctor that everything is starting to look “fuzzy. ”
mcq.answer_text: Cones are the retinal cells that cluster in the fovea and help us have high visual acuity. Rods are found more in the periphery of the retina and specialize in sensing motion. Hair cells and the vestibular system are located in the ear.

mcq.stem: In the course of her examination, the doctor notices that Gwen has particular difficulty detecting colors that correspond with longer wavelengths in the visual spectrum. Which of the following colors is likely to be most difficult for Gwen to see?
mcq.context: Eight-year-old Gwen is beginning to complain of vision problems, so her parents take her to see an eye doctor. Gwen tells the doctor that everything is starting to look “fuzzy. ”
mcq.answer_text: Red waves are the longest in the visual spectrum. The acronym R o y G. B iv gives us the colors in the spectrum from longest to shortest wavelength. White is not a single wavelength but, rather, the combination of the entire visual spectrum.

mcq.context: Mr. Cohen gave his psychology class a quiz on cognitive psychology. This graph shows the distribution of scores in a class of 25 students. Use the distribution shown below to answer the following questions.
mcq.answer_text: In a negatively skewed distribution, there are more high scores than low ones. In this distribution, the one failing score creates a negative skew.

mcq.stem: The median score lies between which values?
mcq.context: Mr. Cohen gave his psychology class a quiz on cognitive psychology. This graph shows the distribution of scores in a class of 25 students. Use the distribution shown below to answer the following questions.
mcq.answer_text: The median score is the middle one in a distribution when scores are listed in ascending or descending order. Seeing as there are 25 scores in this distribution, the 13th score is the median. There are 12 scores below 85 and 4 scores above 95, which means that the 13th score falls between 85 and 94.

mcq.stem: For years, Sutton has suffered from bouts of depression during which she feels very low energy and struggles to complete basic household tasks. She occasionally has an interlude of a few days during which she feels a surge of energy and a sense of optimism and competence, and during those times she functions relatively well. With which of the following disorders would Sutton most likely be diagnosed?
mcq.answer_text: The combination of periods of depression and mania indicate that Sutton suffers from bipolar disorder. The major difference between the two types of bipolar disorder is how severe the depressive and manic periods are. Bipolar I involves more severe periods of mania and fewer periods of depression, while bipolar II involves more depressive periods and occasional periods of mild mania known as hypomania.

mcq.stem: Susana surveys Americans in their 70s and 80s about their contentment with their lives and the number of friends they have. She finds a strong relationship between those two factors and a correlation coefficient of over 0.9. Can she conclude that having a lot of friends leads to contentment in older Americans?

options.A: Yes, because the correlation is so strong
options.B: Yes, because social connections can promote feelings of contentment
options.C: No, because she did not survey every American in this age group
options.D: No, because it’s possible that being content causes people to make more friends

mcq.answer_text: Correlation does not show causation no matter how strong the relationship is between the variables. The directionality problem explains that when two variables are correlated, we cannot tell which one came first and caused the other or if a third variable caused them both.

mcq.stem: Trigger, the beloved dog of the Pearlman family, is terrified of loud noises like thunder and fireworks. He has never been exposed to a traumatic event involving noise, and no amount of training has been able to calm his fears. Trigger’s fear is best explained by which perspective?
mcq.answer_text: Animals and people are predisposed to fear loud noises. From an evolutionary perspective, this fear reflects the idea that many dangerous things, like explosions, are noisy. Fears are often also learned, but the question indicates that nothing happened to Trigger that would have caused him to learn this fear.

mcq.stem: After falling out of a tree and hitting his head, Phineas has trouble walking smoothly. Which letter points to the part of Phineas’s brain most likely to be causing this problem?
mcq.answer_text: K labels the cerebellum, a part of the brain that controls whole-body movements.

mcq.stem: Phineas’s fall also seems to have damaged the area of the brain labeled J. Which of the following symptoms would be the most likely to result from this damage?
mcq.answer_text: The J label is on the medulla oblongata, a structure that regulates autonomic functions like heart and breathing rates.

mcq.stem: If Aaron is most concerned about his performance as compared with that of his peers, which test results will make him happiest?
mcq.context: Aaron took three tests on Wednesday. The table below provides information about his performance and that of his peers. Class Standard Aaron’s Score Class Mean Deviation U.S. History 90 85 2.5 Spanish 86 90 2.0 Algebra 93 87 6.0

In contrast, his score on the Spanish test is 2 standard deviations below the mean, and his score on the algebra test is 1 standard deviation above the mean.

mcq.stem: What’s one way the algebra test differed from the Spanish test?

options.A: The algebra test was harder for Aaron.
options.B: Most students did better on the algebra test.
options.C: Students performed more similarly on the Spanish test.
options.D: The modal performance was higher on the Spanish test.

mcq.answer_text: The relatively low standard deviation on the Spanish test tells us that students performed more similarly to one another on that test as opposed to the algebra test, which had a standard deviation three times as large.

Introduction
The rise of “artificial intelligence” technologies (such as “large
language models” like ChatGPT) started conversations about how
accurately these technologies can reproduce human analysis and
communication about complex topics. An international team of
psychologists decided to test whether these large language
technologies could explain solutions to “moral puzzle” problems.
In addition, they looked at whether human participants would
prefer solutions written by computers or real humans, and
whether they could identify the “author” of the explanations.
Participants
The research team recruited a representative sample of 299 adult

used an internet survey as an initial recruitment strategy. They
shared this post on several social media sites and other sites
designed to reach a large group of internet users. This internet
survey asked potential participants if they might be willing to
participate in a study about moral issues and gathered
demographic information.
Based on the responses to this initial call for participants, the
research team narrowed the list of participants to 299 based on
age, gender, and ethnicity to ensure that the final group of 299
participants were representative of the U.S. adult population
based on these demographic factors. All 299 participants were
informed that if they chose to take the full survey, they would be
paid for their participation, their names and identities would not

Identify the research method used in the study.

”

Part (E)

This study is probably generalizable because the researchers
ensured that the participant group was a representative sample.
The authors said they chose the subjects “based on age, gender,
and ethnicity to ensure that the final group of 299 participants
were representative of the U.S. adult population.” Since the
participant group is a representative sample, this study is probably
generalizable to U.S. adults.
Scoring Guide
In order to get a point for (E), students need to explain why they
think the results of the study are or are not generalizable using
relevant evidence from the research summary.
This response would score 1 point because the student used
relevant evidence—representativeness of the sample—and thus
the findings in this study are probably also true of the larger
population.
Part (F)
Explain how at least one of the research findings supports or refutes
the researchers’ hypothesis that participants would rate computer-
authored responses to moral puzzles as superior in quality when
compared to human-authored responses.
Sample Student Answer
These data support the researchers’ hypothesis about the
“superiority” of the perception of ChatGPT responses over human
responses to these moral puzzles. Since the overall rating on the
5-point scale was 1.4 points higher for computer-authored
responses than the ratings of the human-authored responses (on
a 5-point scale), that’s good evidence in support of the
hypothesis. They also found that this difference was statistically
significant (p < 0.001), meaning that the difference isn’t likely due
to random factors or chance. The authors also included an
argument about why this difference may be happening. They
show that participants can identify which response was written by
ChatGPT, and they suspect that the subjects in the study may
think that ChatGPT is “smarter” or more capable of reasoning
through these puzzles. So participants may rate those responses
as superior.
Scoring Guide
In (F), students can get 1 point for using appropriate evidence but
not having a complete explanation. Students can get 2 points for
using appropriate evidence AND including a complete
argument/explanation for how that evidence shows that the
hypothesis is or is not supported.
This response would score 2 points because the student used
relevant evidence—the higher average superiority ratings for the
ChatGPT responses. The student goes on to summarize the study
authors’ explanation about why these data indicate that the
participants in the study rated the ChatGPT responses as superior.

Introduction
Social psychologists are interested in what interventions might be
likely to reduce prejudiced thinking and behaviors. Since
prejudicial beliefs are often based on expectations built on years
of past experiences, and frequently reinforced by influential
messages on social media sites, it can be difficult to change
people’s prejudicial beliefs and behaviors. Past experiences, media
messages, and peer influences can lead people to develop
prejudicial beliefs about people who they think are in “out-
groups,” and they may behave negatively toward them in
comparison to how they view and behave toward “in-group”
members.
In this meta-analysis, the researchers looked at all the studies
available that investigated the relationship between prejudice and
in-group/out-group bias. Researchers were interested in any
empirical study that used in-group and out-group bias as a
theoretical lens in the discussion about the development of
prejudicial beliefs.
Method
Researchers conducted a comprehensive literature review using
digital journal article databases. After the researchers established
a standardized list of search terms to use across the databases,
they compiled a list of studies to consider for inclusion in the
meta-analysis. The researchers used this list to create inclusion
criteria: elements that must be present in each study for inclusion
in the final meta-analysis. These selection criteria required that
the studies must include at least one comparison group that
resulted in an effect size. These effect sizes were combined across
the studies to produce the final effect sizes reports in Table 1
below as well as the p-values.
Based on the initial search and selection criteria, the researchers
included 22 studies in this meta-analysis. These studies represent
data from more than 8,400 participants worldwide and were
completed between 2002 and 2017.
Results and Discussion
Researchers looked across the 22 prejudice studies identified
during the study selection process. These studies were focused on
several specific variables that researchers suspected might be
relevant to the relationship between prejudice and in-group/out-
group bias. Researchers combined the effect sizes across the
studies in each category and used inferential statistics to
determine whether the effect size was statistically significant by
computing a p-value.

influence in their meta-analytic review was “entativity”—group
cohesion. Based on these results, the researchers predict that the
stronger an individual believes they “belong” in a group and the
more cohesive that group is, the more likely that person may be
to develop prejudicial beliefs about other groups.

Currently, immigration is currently one of the most important, and
most controversial, political discussions in many countries. Many
political parties, policymakers, leaders, and citizens disagree
(sometimes violently) about immigration policies in their countries,

people view levels of prejudice, tolerance for free speech, and
accuracy of their views of the world “within” their group vs. levels

Participants
Researchers recruited participants via a posting on a popular
internet website designed to share online research opportunities
(Amazon Mechanical Turk). Recruitment took place between June
through July, 2017. The online announcement asked anyone
interested in earning $0.75 per response to survey items about

of individuals who filled out the initial online form for the research

Method
Participants in this study read a short text describing an attitude

prejudice, tolerance for free speech, and “truth” (accuracy of

interpretation of the text.
These interpretations included a description of the supposed
author. The author was described either as a member of the
participant’s “in-group” or as a member of the “out-group,” based
on the participant’s self-reported political party—Republican or
Democrat.

Introduction
Social psychologists theorize that prejudicial beliefs are moderated
by the extent to which an individual has contact with different
groups of people (“contact theory”). Previous evidence suggests
that people who do not have frequent contact with other social
groups, including other ethnic/racial groups, may be more prone
to develop prejudicial attitudes about members of these other
groups because of a lack of personal experience and positive
social interactions with people from those demographic groups.
In-group and out-group bias support this possible connection
between lack of exposure and increased prejudicial beliefs.
Introduction
Researchers in this study decided to look at national surveys from
different countries to see if those data provided evidence that
supported or contradicted predictions based on contact theory.
Contact theory would predict that people who belong to social
groups with high levels of diversity and/or who socialize with
people from other demographic groups should express lower
levels of prejudicial beliefs. Some national surveys in specific
countries in the world include questions that allow researchers to
measure both these variables: level of contact with other groups
and prejudicial attitudes.
Participants
The participants in this study were the individuals who
participated in the national surveys. Each of the surveys (see list
in Table 1: National Surveys below) was administered nationwide
in the countries indicated. The items on each of the surveys
differed, but each of these surveys were selected because they
include items that provide data on levels of diversity within social
groups, levels of contact between social groups, and levels of
prejudicial beliefs.
Administration details between the surveys differ slightly, but in
each case the surveys were provided to a large, representative
sample of the target population in that country, either via the mail
or email links to web-based surveys. Participants in the surveys
were provided information before the survey about how the data
would be used and that the survey was anonymous (no names or
other identifying information was gathered by the survey).
Method
Researchers analyzed data from five national surveys that
provided information about levels of contact with other groups

and prejudicial attitudes:
■ European Social Survey
■ 2002 probability survey of the German adult population
■ 2005 national survey of white Americans
■ White British respondents in a 2009–2010 national survey in
England
■ 2011 city survey in Cape Town, South Africa

in each survey that were measures of the following variables:
■ Levels of diversity within social group: each survey asked
participants to describe their family, friend group, and other
social groups they “belong” to. Responses to these items
were used to calculate a score for this variable.

mcq.stem: What is the median number of dollars it took Ms. Rashid’s children to learn to make their beds?
mcq.context: Ms. Rashid has six children: Aaron, Aubrey, Audrey, Annie, Alfred, and Alexa. When they turn five, she teaches them how to make their beds. For the first three, she checked their rooms every day to see if their beds were made and gave them $1 if they were, but for the last three children she only checked every Saturday. The table below shows how many times each child needed to be given a dollar and therefore how much they earned before they learned to make their bed consistently. Number of Dollars Paid to Each Child Checking Schedule Child Aaron Daily 8 Aubrey Daily 6 Audrey Daily 11 Number of Dollars Paid to Each Child Checking Schedule Child Annie Weekly 7 Alfred Weekly 16 Alexa Weekly 12
mcq.answer_text: The median is the middle number when values are ordered by size. When listed this way, the data set looks like 6, 7, 8, 11, 12, 16. Because there are an even number of values, there is no one middle number. So we need to average the middle two numbers, which are 8 and 11. The median is 8 + 11 = 19/2 = 9.5.

mcq.stem: What might explain why the children checked daily learned faster than the children checked weekly?

options.A: Continuous reinforcement typically results in faster learning than intermittent reinforcement.
options.B: The older children probably helped teach the younger ones to make their beds.
options.C: Variable schedules are more resistant to extinction.
options.D: Ms. Rashid probably became used to a more authoritarian parenting style as she got older.

mcq.answer_text: Continuous reinforcement is most effective in teaching new skills. If a child receives a dollar every time they make their bed, they quickly learn that association. If they have to wait a week for the reward, it will take longer for them to link the action and result.

mcq.stem: Cyan has come up with a test to identify people with the potential to be great civil rights lawyers. Such a test would be classified as a(n)
mcq.answer_text: Cyan’s test would be classified as an aptitude test because it is intended to show a person’s potential to be a great civil rights attorney. A speed test is comprised of many items and is meant to demonstrate how quickly a person can answer questions. An achievement test measures people’s knowledge of a given area. An EQ test would measure emotional intelligence.

mcq.stem: Approximately what percent of the population scores between 70 and 130 on the WISC?
mcq.answer_text: Approximately 95 percent of the population scores between 70 and 130 on the WISC. The WISC has a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15, which means that the scores between 70 and 130 represent all the scores within 2 standard deviations of the mean.

mcq.stem: Young Tina had never seen the space shuttle until her parents pointed out a picture of it ready to launch. When she next saw a picture of it flying, she had difficulty recognizing it. Which concept best explains this problem?
mcq.answer_text: Young Tina had never seen the space shuttle until her parents pointed out a picture of it ready to launch. When she next saw a picture of it flying, she had difficulty recognizing it. Tina’s problem can best be explained by shape constancy. Shape constancy is a perceptual constancy that we learn from experience. An unfamiliar object looks different from different angles, and we have to learn that it is the same object. Until we do, we make errors like Tina’s. The autokinetic effect is when a spot of light in a dark room appears to move on its own. Dishabituation refers to an increase in response that occurs to a novel stimulus. Summation refers to the way the layers of the retina are set up: multiple rods and cones synapse with one bipolar cell, and multiple bipolar cells synapse with a single ganglion cell.

mcq.stem: Alyssa presents one group of shoppers with an advertisement for milk that is 99 percent fat free and another group of shoppers with an advertisement for milk that is 1 percent fat. What is Alyssa most likely testing?
mcq.answer_text: Alyssa is testing the impact of framing. Milk that is 1 percent fat is the same as milk that is 99 percent fat free; the only difference is how the milk is framed. Representativeness heuristic is when people judge the likelihood of an event by comparing it to something they believe to be similar and assuming the probabilities of the events will be the same. Confirmation bias is the tendency to pay more attention to information that supports our preexisting beliefs than information that contradicts it. Schema are cognitive structures that influence how we process information.

mcq.stem: Jupiter pilots his newly created perfectionism scale on a high school psychology class. He returns one month later to administer the same test to the same students, and then he correlates the two sets of results. What is Jupiter probably doing?

options.C: Looking to see if the mean level of perfectionism has changed

mcq.answer_text: In correlating the two sets of results, Jupiter is measuring the test’s reliability. This type of reliability is known as test-retest reliability. Since perfectionism should not change over the course of the month, a low correlation would indicate that the test was not reliable. Outliers are extreme scores, and Jupiter does not appear to be looking for them. To standardize the test, Jupiter would have to give it to a standardization sample and then look to assemble a group of questions that yielded a normal distribution of scores. Nothing in the question suggests Jupiter believes the mean level of perfectionism should have changed, and the correlation will not necessarily show whether it has.

mcq.stem: If the College Board neglected to put any questions that had to do with neuroscience on the AP Psychology exam one year, the test would lack
mcq.answer_text: If the College Board neglected to put any questions that had to do with neuroscience on the AP Psychology exam one year, the test would lack content validity. A valid test measures what it is supposed to measure. A test with high content validity covers all the areas it is supposed to in the appropriate level of depth. Predictive and concurrent validity are two types of criterion validity. A test with predictive validity provides a measure of how someone will perform on a task in the future, whereas concurrent validity provides a measure of how someone will perform at the present time. Construct validity, choice (A), is a term that applies to tests that attempt to measure one overall idea or construct, not a test like the AP Psychology exam that measures many different areas of knowledge.

Because it was unlikely that Trigger was going to wake up one morning and trot out to get the paper, Andrea reinforced steps toward that end goal—going toward the paper, touching the paper with his mouth, and so on.
